record.paper_title: Open questions in massive star research
record.original_question: Are luminous blue variable stars physically close to their Eddington limit, with their observed large radius and brightness variations driven by inflated envelopes that cannot settle into thermal equilibrium under plausible mass-loss prescriptions? If so, does the same Eddington-limit physics also explain giant eruptions like η Carinae's, or are those eruptions instead products of stellar mergers in very massive multiple systems?

evidence.quote: 3.2. Are Luminous Blue Variable stars near their Eddington limit?
Whether the great LBV eruptions `a la η Carina also relate to the Eddington limit is not clear yet.
More 3D models of binary mergers (Schneider et al. 2019) are needed to systematically study their mass outflows, and to investigate their features when they occur near the Eddington limit.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Consider a very massive star (initial mass ≳ 25 M☉) whose surface luminosity L is comparable to its classical Eddington luminosity L_Edd = 4πGMc/κ, where M is the stellar mass and κ the relevant opacity (in particular the iron opacity peak in the subsurface layers). Such a star is called a Luminous Blue Variable (LBV) if it exhibits irregular photometric and spectroscopic variability, including S Doradus–type excursions in which the apparent radius and effective temperature change by large factors at roughly constant bolometric luminosity, and occasional "giant eruptions" (as exemplified historically by the 19th-century outburst of η Carinae) in which several solar masses of material are ejected on timescales of years to decades.

(a) Are LBVs in their variable state physically located close to the Eddington limit, in the sense that the proximity L/L_Edd → 1 in their envelopes is the dynamical cause of their large radius and brightness variations? More precisely, do their observed S Doradus variations arise from radiation-pressure-driven inflated envelopes that, under any astrophysically plausible mass-loss prescription Ṁ(L,M,R,Z,…), fail to settle into a hydrostatic and thermal equilibrium configuration?

(b) If the answer to (a) is affirmative, does the same Eddington-limit / inflated-envelope mechanism also account for giant LBV eruptions of the η Carinae type, producing the observed eruptive mass loss (∼10 M☉ on decadal timescales) and light curve? Or are such giant eruptions instead produced by a fundamentally different mechanism — namely stellar mergers (or common-envelope events) within very massive multiple systems — whose 3D hydrodynamic outcomes near the Eddington limit reproduce the observed energetics, ejecta masses, geometries, and circumstellar nebulae (e.g., the bipolar Homunculus of η Carinae)?
artifact.category_tag: Stellar astrophysics — LBVs and Eddington-limit instabilities
artifact.status_search_result: The physical origin of LBV variability and giant eruptions remains an actively debated open problem. Reviews and recent modeling work agree that LBVs sit close to the Eddington limit and that envelope inflation associated with the iron opacity peak is a leading explanation for S Doradus variability, but no mass-loss prescription has been shown to produce a unique consistent equilibrium. For η Carinae's Great Eruption, both Eddington-limit/continuum-driven wind models and binary/triple merger scenarios (e.g., Portegies Zwart & van den Heuvel; Smith; Hirai et al.) remain viable competing hypotheses, with no consensus as of 2024–2026.

status_evidence.title: Luminous Blue Variables (MDPI Galaxies review)
status_evidence.snippet: LBVs are near the Eddington limit; S Dor variations are likely caused by envelope inflation or pulsation linked to the subsurface Fe opacity peak; mass-loss rates in S Dor maxima are too low to form large pseudo-photospheres.
status_evidence.claim: LBV variability mechanism (Eddington-limit inflated envelope vs. wind pseudo-photosphere) is still under active investigation.

status_evidence.title: Was the nineteenth century giant eruption of Eta Carinae a merger event in a triple system? (MNRAS)
status_evidence.snippet: Proposes that η Carinae's Great Eruption resulted from a merger in an originally triple system, as an alternative to single-star Eddington-limit instabilities.
status_evidence.claim: Merger origin for η Car-like giant eruptions is a competing, unresolved hypothesis.

status_evidence.title: Luminous Blue Variables and Superluminous Supernovae from Binary Mergers (ApJ)
status_evidence.snippet: Argues that some LBVs and their eruptions can be products of binary mergers in massive systems.
status_evidence.claim: Binary-merger channel for LBV eruptions remains an active alternative explanation.

status_evidence.title: Luminous blue variables and the fates of very massive stars (PMC)
status_evidence.snippet: Reviews open questions about LBV mass loss, eruptions, and connection to supernovae; mechanism of giant eruptions not settled.
status_evidence.claim: Giant LBV eruption mechanism remains an open question.
